name: Old Hall Hotel
subject: Royal visits
text: Mary, Queen of Scots came to Buxton to bathe in the warm spring water. She lodged at the Hall during visits between 1573 and 1584. Part of the fortified tower survives inside the later hotel.

source.title: High Peak Borough Council — Buxton conservation area

name: Boscobel House
subject: Royal visits
text: In 1651 this hunting lodge was a hiding place for Charles II after his defeat at Worcester. The oak in which he hid became part of the escape story remembered in the pub name Royal Oak.

name: Magpie Mine
subject: Mines and quarries
text: The walls on this hillside enclose the workings of five lead mines. Magpie was only one of them. Its neighbours had names such as Dirty Red Soil and Horsesteps.

name: Big Pit National Coal Museum
subject: Mines and quarries
text: Big Pit worked as a coal mine from 1880 until 1980. Just three years later it opened as a museum, giving the workings a second life.

name: Wieliczka Salt Mine
subject: Mines and quarries
text: Salt shaped this town long before miners sank shafts here. People first collected it from brine rising to the surface, and in the thirteenth century miners began cutting into the salt below.

name: Millers Dale railway station
subject: Old railways
text: Miller’s Dale station opened in 1863. Passengers for Buxton could change trains here. The platforms now sit beside a trail where trains once ran between Manchester and London.

name: Monsal Trail
subject: Old railways
text: The level track through these limestone dales was built for trains. Today the Monsal Trail follows part of the Midland Railway route that once connected Manchester with London.

name: Cromford Mills
subject: Mills
text: In 1771 Richard Arkwright established a cotton-spinning mill at Cromford. Water supplied the power to turn the machines, which helps explain why a factory of such influence was built here.

name: New Lanark
subject: Mills
text: David Dale built cotton mills beside the River Clyde and houses for the people who would work in them. The village and its industry grew together from the 1780s.

name: Litton Mill
subject: Mills
text: The River Wye once supplied the power to spin cotton at Litton Mill. The business was founded in 1782 by Ellis Needham and Thomas Frith.

name: Quarry Bank Mill
subject: Mills
text: Quarry Bank began spinning cotton in 1784. The mill and the workers’ village at Styal preserve two sides of the same story: the machinery and the people who kept it running.

name: Pontcysyllte Aqueduct
subject: Rivers and bridges
text: Boats cross the River Dee here without descending to it. The Llangollen Canal runs high overhead in a cast-iron trough carried on nineteen arches.

name: Pont du Gard
subject: Rivers and bridges
text: This Roman bridge carried drinking water across the Gardon on its way to Nîmes. It was one crossing on an aqueduct roughly fifty kilometres long.

name: Chee Dale
subject: Woods and nature reserves
text: The River Wye threads a narrow limestone gorge at Chee Dale. Above it the former railway skirts the cliffs, giving walkers a very different view of the valley from the riverside path.

name: Padley Gorge
subject: Woods and nature reserves
text: Burbage Brook runs through the woods at Padley Gorge. It once marked the county boundary between Derbyshire and Yorkshire.

name: Wistman's Wood
subject: Woods and nature reserves
text: The twisted oaks of Wistman’s Wood grow high on Dartmoor. They are part of a surviving patch of temperate rainforest in a landscape many people picture as open moor.

name: Poole's Cavern
subject: Geology
text: Buxton’s limestone landscape continues underground. Poole’s Cavern belongs to the Wye cave system, where water has shaped a passage beneath the hillside.

name: Blue John Cavern
subject: Geology
text: Blue John is a coloured variety of fluorite. The cavern near Castleton owes its name to the mineral that people came underground to extract.

name: Giant's Causeway
subject: Geology
text: The interlocking columns along this coast formed as volcanic rock cooled and contracted. There are roughly forty thousand of them.

name: Wharram Percy
subject: Deserted medieval villages
text: The ruined church is the easiest building to spot at Wharram Percy. The village is still visible in the grass above it, where low earthworks trace the outlines of houses.

name: Gainsthorpe
subject: Deserted medieval villages
text: An open field at Gainsthorpe preserves the layout of a medieval village. The humps and hollows mark lanes, plots and buildings that disappeared above ground centuries ago.

name: Devonshire Dome
subject: Former uses of buildings
text: Buxton’s great dome grew out of a stable block. The building later housed a hospital, and architect Robert Rippon Duke added the wide unsupported dome over the former courtyard.

name: Tate Modern
subject: Former uses of buildings
text: Bankside’s power station became Tate Modern. The Turbine Hall takes its name from the machines that once generated electricity in the space now used to display art.

name: Musée d'Orsay
subject: Former uses of buildings
text: This museum beside the Seine began as a railway terminus. The former Gare d’Orsay now houses paintings and sculpture beneath the roof that once covered arriving trains.

name: York Watergate
subject: Street features
text: The York Watergate once opened directly onto the Thames. It now stands inland in Victoria Embankment Gardens, a surviving clue to where the riverbank used to be.

name: London Stone
subject: Street features
text: A small block of limestone on Cannon Street is the surviving fragment of a much larger landmark. London Stone stood for centuries on the other side of the street.

name: River Sheaf
subject: Hidden waterways
text: The River Sheaf disappears into a culvert beneath central Sheffield. It continues below the city streets until it joins the River Don.

name: River Fleet
subject: Hidden waterways
text: The Fleet still flows beneath London. During the nineteenth century its lower course became part of the sewer system, hiding a river that had once reached the Thames in the open.

name: Doune Castle
subject: Filming locations
text: Doune Castle played Castle Leoch, home of Clan MacKenzie, in Outlander. The same Scottish castle also appeared in Monty Python and the Holy Grail.

name: Glenfinnan Viaduct
subject: Filming locations
text: Trains on the West Highland Line curve across this viaduct above Loch Shiel. Film audiences know the crossing from the Hogwarts Express scenes in the Harry Potter films.

name: Hobbiton Movie Set
subject: Filming locations
text: A farm in New Zealand stood in for the Shire in The Lord of the Rings. The filmmakers returned to create Hobbiton again for The Hobbit films.

name: Tissington Trail
subject: Walking
text: The walking and cycling trail follows the trackbed of the railway between Ashbourne and Buxton. Its name comes from Tissington, the village the line skirts.

name: Water of Leith Walkway
subject: Walking
text: This path follows Edinburgh’s river from Balerno to Leith. Walking it links parts of the city that look quite separate from the roads above.

name: Bass Rock
subject: Animal stories
text: The steep island rising out of the Firth of Forth is a volcanic plug. Its rocky slopes support a colony of northern gannets.

name: Skomer
subject: Animal stories
text: Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on Skomer. The island’s puffins are easier for daytime visitors to spot, although both birds breed on the same small island.

name: Longleat Safari and Adventure Park
subject: Animal stories
text: Longleat opened its drive-through safari park in 1966, in the grounds of the Wiltshire country house. It brought the experience of watching animals from a vehicle to an English estate.

name: Down House
subject: Famous people
text: Charles Darwin worked on natural selection in this house and its garden. The grounds were part of his working life as a scientist as well as his family home.

name: Dove Cottage
subject: Famous people
text: William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy moved into Dove Cottage in 1799. The small house in Grasmere was their home for more than eight years.

name: St George's Hall, Liverpool
subject: Important buildings
text: Behind this Liverpool landmark’s classical façade are both concert halls and law courts. The building opened in 1854, bringing music and court proceedings under the same roof.

name: Buxton Opera House
subject: Important buildings
text: Frank Matcham designed Buxton Opera House, which opened in 1903. Its place on the square puts a purpose-built theatre alongside the town’s gardens and spa buildings.

name: Skara Brae
subject: Neolithic archaeology
text: A storm exposed stone buildings beneath the sand at Skara Brae. The Neolithic settlement preserves the arrangement of homes facing a network of passages.

name: West Kennet Long Barrow
subject: Neolithic archaeology
text: People in Early Neolithic Wiltshire built stone chambers under this long mound. The chambers made the interior a place people could enter again.

name: Castell Henllys
subject: Iron Age archaeology
text: The Iron Age hillfort at Castell Henllys has reconstructed roundhouses. Archaeologists used evidence from excavations to place them on the footprints of earlier buildings.

name: Maiden Castle, Dorset
subject: Iron Age archaeology
text: The banks and ditches near Dorchester enclosed an Iron Age hillfort. The hill had already been used thousands of years earlier, in the Neolithic period.

name: Navio Roman Fort
subject: Roman archaeology
text: The Roman fort at Brough overlooks a bend in the River Noe. A civilian settlement grew beside the military site, which was linked by road to Buxton.

name: Nine Ladies
subject: Late Neolithic and Bronze Age archaeology
text: The low stones on Stanton Moor form a prehistoric circle. The Nine Ladies belong to a stone-circle tradition spanning the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age.

name: The Crown Inn, Chiddingfold
subject: Royal visits
text: On 21 July 1552 Edward VI and his travelling court came to Chiddingfold. They camped on the village green facing the Crown Inn.

source.title: Waverley Borough Council — Chiddingfold conservation area

name: Peak Forest Tramway
subject: Old railways
text: Horses and gravity powered the Peak Forest Tramway when it began trading in 1796. Part of its western course survives as a walking trail.

name: The Bull Ring
subject: Late Neolithic archaeology
text: The ring at Dove Holes is an earthwork built in the Late Neolithic period. Close beside the henge are two burial mounds of different shapes, one oval and one round.

name: Brooklyn Bridge
subject: Rivers and bridges
text: When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883 it gave Manhattan and Brooklyn their first fixed crossing of the East River. The main span was then the longest of any suspension bridge in the world.

name: Great Zimbabwe
subject: Medieval archaeology
text: The stone city near Masvingo grew into a royal capital from the thirteenth century. Its builders were ancestors of the Shona people, who had settled here centuries earlier.

name: Petrified Forest National Park
subject: Geology
text: The wood that gives this Arizona park its name has turned to stone. Deposits of petrified timber survive among the coloured badlands of a landscape that now looks quite different from a forest.

name: Vera Brittain’s home on Park Road
subject: Commemorative plaques
text: In 1907 the Brittain family moved to Melrose, the house now numbered 151 Park Road. Vera was still living in Buxton in 1915, when she left for London to nurse. The plaque marks the family home.

name: Leawood Pump House
subject: Industrial heritage
text: The Cromford Canal needed a way to top up its water. This engine house used a steam-powered beam engine built in 1849 to lift water from the River Derwent into the canal.

name: Bell Mill, Stanley Mills
subject: Industrial heritage
text: The bend in the River Tay explains why a cotton mill was built here in 1786. Its machinery could draw power from the river. Textile production at Stanley Mills lasted roughly two centuries.

name: Ballycopeland Windmill
subject: Industrial heritage
text: This County Down windmill worked until the First World War. Bringing it back into working order took a generation: restoration began in 1950 and continued until 1978.

name: Blaenavon Ironworks
subject: Industrial heritage
text: Alongside the blast furnaces stands a tower built for lifting loads using the weight of water. Workers’ cottages survive at the ironworks too, putting the homes of the people who worked here beside the machinery.

name: Mount Sunday — Edoras
subject: Filming locations
text: This Canterbury hill became Edoras, the hilltop capital of Rohan in The Lord of the Rings. The film buildings were taken away afterwards. The shape of Mount Sunday and the mountains around it are what you can recognise today.

name: Himeji Castle
subject: Filming locations
text: James Bond and Akira Kurosawa share a filming location here. Himeji Castle appeared in You Only Live Twice and was also used in Kurosawa’s films Ran and Kagemusha.

source.title: National Film Archive of Japan location database
